definition: In social psychology, justification means the reasons people use to explain, defend, or make sense of a behavior or attitude. In this source, justifications for meat-eating are treated as psychologically meaningful beliefs that are strongly related to meat-eating and to views such as social dominance orientation, speciesism, and masculinity.

reasons: The first sentence (“In social psychology, justification means the reasons people use to explain, defend, or make sense of a behavior or attitude”) is not supported by the provided packet text.
The packet does not state that justifications for meat-eating are “psychologically meaningful beliefs”; it only describes “meat-eating justification scales” and associations.

Claims about which specific related views (social dominance orientation, speciesism, masculinity) are tied to “justifications” are only indirectly supported; the packet only says it replicates associations between meat-eating, “its justifications,” and those constructs, without supporting the additional phrasing about what “justifications” are (e.g., beliefs).

The packet supports meat-eating justifications and their associations with meat-eating, social dominance orientation, speciesism, and masculinity, but it does not support the broad general definition of justification as reasons people use to explain, defend, or make sense of behavior or attitudes.
The phrase "psychologically meaningful beliefs" is an unsupported characterization not stated in the packet.
